title: Iterating Consistency Models: Stability, Error Bounds and Noise Schedules

paper.title: Iterating Consistency Models: Stability, Error Bounds and Noise Schedules
paper.abstract:
Abstract Consistency models (CMs) have become a leading approach for generating
high-quality samples in few steps. However, adding steps can improve or degrade
sample quality in ways that are highly sensitive to the schedule and that
existing theory does not fully explain. To provide accuracy guarantees and guide CM sampler design, we analyze multistep CM sampling as a composition of noising and approximate denoising operators. Under explicit, verifiable stability
assumptions, we derive a non-asymptotic error bound that separates
contraction of the initialization error from accumulation of approximation
error. The bound assigns distinct roles to the schedule: large early noise
levels drive contraction, while small late noise levels control the
residual bias. As a corollary, we obtain explicit constants for
strongly log-concave and semi-log-concave targets. We further establish a complementary guarantee whose assumptions, one-step accuracy and stability, can be estimated for a given trained model. Experiments show that the
contraction and approximation profiles entering our bounds can be reliably
measured and closely match the predicted functional forms. Together, these
results provide a meaningful convergence theory for multi-step CMs and a
practical route to sampler design.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models (DMs) ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Song & Ermon, 2019 ; Song et al., 2021 ; Ho et al., 2020 ) have revolutionized generative machine learning, achieving remarkable results in image ( Ramesh et al., 2022 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ) , video ( Ho et al., 2022 ; Blattmann et al., 2023 ; Wan et al., 2025 ) , 3D ( Liu et al., 2023b ; Poole et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) , and audio generation ( Evans et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2023a ) . Early DMs required hundreds to thousands of neural function evaluations (NFEs) per sample. However, distillation substantially reduces this cost, such as direct ( Luhman & Luhman, 2021 ; Zheng et al., 2022 ) , adversarial ( Wang et al., 2022 ; Sauer et al., 2024 ) , or variational score distillation ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Yin et al., 2024b ; Yin et al., 2024a ; Luo et al., 2023b ; Salimans et al., 2024 ) . Within this context, consistency models (CMs) ( Song et al., 2023 ; Song & Dhariwal, 2023 ; Kim et al., 2023 ) have emerged as particularly effective few-step DMs. A CM learns a consistency function that maps noisy points along a probability-flow ODE trajectory directly to clean data. It can be distilled from a pre-trained DM (consistency distillation) or trained from scratch (consistency training). Training CMs is nonetheless delicate. Discrete-time training introduces a discretization error that degrades sample quality, whereas naive continuous-time training is notoriously unstable ( Song et al., 2023 ; Song & Dhariwal, 2023 ; Geng et al., 2024 ) . sCM ( Lu & Song, 2025 ) addressed this with TrigFlow, a formulation that greatly improves stability. A closely related line of work ( Geng et al., 2025 ; Sabour et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ) learns flow maps ( Boffi et al., 2025a ) , which transport samples between any two points of the trajectory and include CMs as an important special case. Methods such as IMM ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) , MeanFlow ( Geng et al., 2025 ) , and SCoT ( Wu et al., 2025 ) make training more stable still by adding constraints to the learning objective. In principle, CMs can generate a sample with a single network evaluation, but practical samplers often apply the model several times to improve sample quality. Each iteration re-noises the current sample and maps it back to the target with the learned consistency function. Multistep CMs, however, are brittle: additional steps do not always help, sample quality is highly sensitive to the noise schedule, and stopping early sometimes yields better samples than continuing. Existing theory for multistep samplers is limited and offers little guidance to practitioners designing or deploying CMs. Intuitively, multistep CM sampling trades off two competing effects. On the one hand, each additional step can reduce the discrepancy between the generated and target distributions. On the other hand, each step introduces a new error from model bias. The key question is thus whether the contraction gained at each step outweighs the error it introduces. This paper makes that balance explicit. To this end, we study multistep samplers that alternately apply stochastic noising and deterministic denoising operators to probability distributions. Our main contribution is a non-asymptotic convergence theory for multistep CMs that explains how the schedule governs sample quality and provides a principled basis for sampler design. Specifically: • Error bound and the role of the schedule. We derive a non-asymptotic error bound that separates contraction of the initialization error from accumulated approximation error. The schedule plays two roles: large early steps drive contraction, while small late steps control the residual bias. For strongly log-concave and semi-log-concave targets, we obtain explicit constants. • Guarantees for trained CMs. We provide a complementary guarantee whose assumptions, one-step accuracy and stability of the learned map, can be estimated for any trained model. • Empirical validation. Experiments show that the contraction and approximation profiles in our bounds can be measured reliably and closely match the functional forms predicted by our theory.

sections.heading: Relation to existing work.
sections.text: Convergence theory for CM sampling is recent. Lyu et al. (2024) analyze one-step and multistep sampling under Ornstein–Uhlenbeck noising. Assuming that the learned map is Lipschitz and that the score and consistency training errors are small, they bound the Wasserstein error of the sampler and show that repeating a suitable noise level reduces this error geometrically, down to a plateau set by the training errors. Chen et al. (2025) derive multistep guarantees for bounded targets via a Kullback–Leibler recursion, and other work addresses statistical accuracy and consistency training ( Dou et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . We build on the error recursion of Lyu et al. (2024) but establish its ingredients under different assumptions. First, as they suggest, we place the stability condition required for contraction on the exact denoiser rather than on the learned network, and show that it holds under natural conditions on the target, such as semi-log-concavity. Second, we allow general Gaussian noising processes and arbitrary schedules. Third, we adopt a more realistic error model in which the score error may diverge as the noise level tends to zero ( De Bortoli, 2022 , Assumption A3) , where noising no longer smooths the target, rather than remaining uniformly small. We make the correspondence between the two sets of results precise after Proposition 3.1 , in Section 3.3 , and in Appendix C .

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: This paper derived a finite-horizon W 2 W_{2} recursion for multistep CM sampling that separates contraction of the initialization error from accumulation of approximation error. Placing stability on the exact denoiser makes the contraction factor q t q_{t} a property of the target, explicit under strong log-concavity and, above a noise threshold, under semi-log-concavity. Under a balance condition, the recursion yields a sharp geometric bound, and a complementary guarantee extends it to trained CMs under estimable assumptions. The experiments corroborate this analysis, as the estimated profiles closely follow the predicted functional forms. Future work includes extending the analysis to zero-shot samplers with inference-time guidance or rewards Spagnoletti et al. (2025) , and optimizing schedules directly from the bound.

This needs a variance error entering the step in the direction opposite to the one the step creates. However, adding steps can improve or degrade sample quality in ways that are highly sensitive to the schedule and that existing theory does not fully explain. To provide accuracy guarantees and guide CM sampler design, we analyze multistep CM sampling as a composition of noising and approximate denoising operators. Under explicit, verifiable stability assumptions, we derive a non-asymptotic error bound that separates contraction of the initialization error from accumulation of approximation error. The bound assigns distinct roles to the schedule: large early noise levels drive contraction, while small late noise levels control the residual bias. As a corollary, we obtain explicit constants for strongly log-concave and semi-log-concave targets. We further establish a complementary guarantee whose assumptions, one-step accuracy and stability, can be estimated for a given trained model. Experiments show that the contraction and approximation profiles entering our bounds can be reliably measured and closely match the predicted functional forms. Together, these results provide a meaningful convergence theory for multi-step CMs and a practical route to sampler design. 1 Introduction Diffusion models (DMs) ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Song & Ermon, 2019 ; Song et al., 2021 ; Ho et al., 2020 ) have revolutionized generative machine learning, achieving remarkable results in image ( Ramesh et al., 2022 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ) , video ( Ho et al., 2022 ; Blattmann et al., 2023 ; Wan et al., 2025 ) , 3D ( Liu et al., 2023b ; Poole et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) , and audio generation ( Evans et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2023a ) . Early DMs required hundreds to thousands of neural function evaluations (NFEs) per sample. However, distillation substantially reduces this cost, such as direct ( Luhman & Luhman, 2021 ; Zheng et al., 2022 ) , adversarial ( Wang et al., 2022 ; Sauer et al., 2024 ) , or variational score distillation ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Yin et al., 2024b ; Yin et al., 2024a ; Luo et al., 2023b ; Salimans et al., 2024 ) . Within this context, consistency models (CMs) ( Song et al., 2023 ; Song & Dhariwal, 2023 ; Kim et al., 2023 ) have emerged as particularly effective few-step DMs. A CM learns a consistency function that maps noisy points along a probability-flow ODE trajectory directly to clean data. It can be distilled from a pre-trained DM (consistency distillation) or trained from scratch (consistency training). Training CMs is nonetheless delicate. Discrete-time training introduces a discretization error that degrades sample quality, whereas naive continuous-time training is notoriously unstable ( Song et al., 2023 ; Song & Dhariwal, 2023 ; Geng et al., 2024 ) . sCM ( Lu & Song, 2025 ) addressed this with TrigFlow, a formulation that greatly improves stability. A closely related line of work ( Geng et al., 2025 ; Sabour et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ) learns flow maps ( Boffi et al., 2025a ) , which transport samples between any two points of the trajectory and include CMs as an important special case. Methods such as IMM ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) , MeanFlow ( Geng et al., 2025 ) , and SCoT ( Wu et al., 2025 ) make training more stable still by adding constraints to the learning objective. In principle, CMs can generate a sample with a single network evaluation, but practical samplers often apply the model several times to improve sample quality. Each iteration re-noises the current sample and maps it back to the target with the learned consistency function. Multistep CMs, however, are brittle: additional steps do not always help, sample quality is highly sensitive to the noise schedule, and stopping early sometimes yields better samples than continuing. Existing theory for multistep samplers is limited and offers little guidance to practitioners designing or deploying CMs. Intuitively, multistep CM sampling trades off two competing effects. On the one hand, each additional step can reduce the discrepancy between the generated and target distributions. On the other hand, each step introduces a new error from model bias. The key question is thus whether the contraction gained at each step outweighs the error it introduces. This paper makes that balance explicit. To this end, we study multistep samplers that alternately apply stochastic noising and deterministic denoising operators to probability distributions. Our main contribution is a non-asymptotic convergence theory for multistep CMs that explains how the schedule governs sample quality and provides a principled basis for sampler design. Specifically: • Error bound and the role of the schedule. We derive a non-asymptotic error bound that separates contraction of the initialization error from accumulated approximation error. The schedule plays two roles: large early steps drive contraction, while small late steps control the residual bias. For strongly log-concave and semi-log-concave targets, we obtain explicit constants. • Guarantees for trained CMs. We provide a complementary guarantee whose assumptions, one-step accuracy and stability of the learned map, can be estimated for any trained model. • Empirical validation. Experiments show that the contraction and approximation profiles in our bounds can be measured reliably and closely match the functional forms predicted by our theory. Relation to existing work. Convergence theory for CM sampling is recent. Lyu et al. (2024) analyze one-step and multistep sampling under Ornstein–Uhlenbeck noising. Assuming that the learned map is Lipschitz and that the score and consistency training errors are small, they bound the Wasserstein error of the sampler and show that repeating a suitable noise level reduces this error geometrically, down to a plateau set by the training errors. Chen et al. (2025) derive multistep guarantees for bounded targets via a Kullback–Leibler recursion, and other work addresses statistical accuracy and consistency training ( Dou et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . We build on the error recursion of Lyu et al. (2024) but establish its ingredients under different assumptions.
